opts.t: Confrontation — point out an inconsistency calmly
Interpretation — restate what you think they mean
Explanation — tell them what is happening
Summary — repeat main points

q: You say, "It sounds like you're worried this is a heart attack." What communication type is that?

opts.t: Interpretation — restate what you think they mean
Confrontation — inconsistency
Explanation — what you are doing
Summary — recap the story
opts.why: Summary is the two-hour walking-pain recap.

q: You say, "I'm putting this oxygen mask on to help you breathe." What communication type is that?

opts.t: Explanation — tell them what is happening
Summary — repeat the history
Confrontation — point out inconsistency
False reassurance — a listed thing to avoid
opts.why: You are explaining a real action.

q: You say, "Pain for two hours, started while walking, worse with deep breaths — correct?" What communication type is that?

opts.t: Summary — briefly repeat the main points
Leading question — listed as something to avoid
opts.why: You are confirming their story, not planting the answer.

opts.t: Giving advice
opts.why: You are not telling them what to do.

opts.t: Judgmental statement

q: "Don't worry you're going to be completely fine," leading questions, giving advice, jargon, and judgmental statements. What list is that?

opts.t: The communication avoid list
opts.why: Those are the listed things to avoid.

opts.t: Open-ended questions like What happened?
The golden-rule items: eye contact and the patient's proper name
The hearing-impaired golden rule: face them so they can read your lips

q: Eye contact, introduce yourself, use their proper name, tell the truth, use language they understand, watch body language, speak slowly and clearly, and face hearing-impaired patients. Which pair finishes the 10 golden rules?

opts.t: Give them time to answer; use a calm confident manner
opts.why: Those finish the 10 golden rules for calming and reassuring.

opts.t: Talk over them with your partner and use jargon
opts.why: Those are on the avoid list.

opts.t: Give advice and leading questions first
Say their full name over the radio as a courtesy
opts.why: Do not say the patient's name over the radio.

q: Radio traffic should be brief, clear, professional, and plain English. What else belongs?

opts.t: Do not say the patient's name over the radio; repeat orders back to confirm
opts.why: No names on the radio. Repeat orders back.

opts.t: Always use 10-codes; they are listed in full
opts.why: 10-codes and local templates are not listed; use plain English unless required.

opts.t: Say the patient's name twice so the hospital can chart it
opts.why: Do not say the name on the radio.

opts.t: Never repeat a physician order — just guess if you missed it

opts.why: It is a permanent legal record.

opts.t: Opinions and judgments are preferred over facts
Treatments and times are optional

opts.t: If it isn't documented, it didn't happen

opts.t: You may skip the PCR if the verbal handoff was friendly

opts.t: The PCR can wait until next shift if you already spoke
opts.why: The PCR is part of official transfer.

q: You made an error on the PCR. How do you correct it?

opts.why: Line through, initial, date, correct. Never erase or cover up.

Start a new PCR and shred the old one quietly

opts.t: Abduction is palm up; flexion is head turning
